source_text: CAPUT QUINTUM, De statu animae a corpore separata. Hucusque fuit de animae immortalitate: sequitur illius a corpore separatio, quae justo Dei judicio manet omnes Adae posteros, tam divites quam pauperes, tam pietate conspicuos quam impios & sceleratos: unde novus animae status exoritur, qui separationis vulgo dicitur. Nam ex quo primi parentes, quibus a Deo dictum erat, Quocunque die comederis de fructu hoc, morte morieris, mandatum Dei violarunt, non tantum sibi moriendi necessitatem attraxerunt, sed & posteris universis, ut testatur Apostolus Rom. 5.12. & 6.23. & 1.Cor. 15.22. & 36. Quibus consentit Sap. 1.13. & 2.24. Exemplum est Luc. 16.22. Hinc concilium Milevitanum anathema dicit can. 1. Pelagianis dicentibus, hominem de corpore exire non peccati merito, sed necessitate naturae. Et Arausicanum 2. can. 2. anathemate ferit eos, qui negant mortem corporis esse poenam peccati.
english: CHAPTER FIVE. On the state of the soul separated from the body.

Hitherto there has been discussion of the immortality of the soul: there follows its separation from the body, which by the just judgment of God awaits all Adam's posterity — rich as well as poor, those conspicuous for piety as well as the impious and wicked: whence a new state of the soul arises, which is commonly called the state of separation.

For from the time when the first parents, to whom it had been said by God, On whatever day you eat of this fruit, you shall die the death, violated God's commandment, they drew upon themselves not only the necessity of dying, but also upon all their posterity, as the Apostle witnesses (Romans 5:12 and 6:23 and 1 Corinthians 15:22 and 36). With which Wisdom 1:13 and 2:24 agree. An example is Luke 16:22.

Hence the Council of Milevis pronounces anathema (canon 1) against the Pelagians who say that a human being goes out from the body not by the desert of sin but by necessity of nature. And the Second Council of Orange (canon 2) strikes with anathema those who deny that the death of the body is the punishment of sin.

source_text: XX. Origenes vero fundamenta jaciens pontificii purgatorii ex dogmate Platonis, a Virgilio quoque 6. Aeneid. expresso, primus in ecclesiam invexit ignem, quo animae post hanc vitam a peccatis purgarentur. XXI. Origenem in hac re secuti Ambrosius, Hilarius, Hieronymus, Rufinus. XXII. Differt tamen purgatorium Origenis a pontificio trifariam. 1. Ratione personarum, quia juxta pontificios duntaxat igni purgantur, quorum animae alicujus temporalis poenae reatu obstructae, vel cum aliquibus peccatis venialibus migrant de hac vita: at juxta Origenem & alios, qui Augustinum praecesserunt, mortales omnes, uno Christo excepto, ignem hunc subibunt. 2. Ratione temporis, quia pontificii animas statim ab excessu, veteres illi non nisi extremo judicii die igni hoc purgandas docent. 3. Ratione mitigationis, quia pontificii censent tolli vel mitigari posse poenas purgatoriales per oblationes & orationes vivorum, quale nihil sensit aut dixit Origenes, vel quos eum secutos delibamus. XXIII. Purgatorium igitur quale tradunt pontificii, ante Augustini tempora ignotum fuit: at Augustino illud dubium visum: a Gregorii vero aetate in Romana ecclesia ex mendacibus revelationibus ac visionibus habitum est certum; Graeca vero ecclesia nec hodie recipit. Haec omnia rectissime infinitae lectionis & doctrinae vir Gerh. Vossius de statu animae separatae adstruxit. Si qua in contrarium ex antiquitate afferuntur, ea sunt vel e scriptis nothis ac spuriis: vel loquuntur de purgatione hujus saeculi, quae fit per ignem tribulationis, ut Augustinus: vel de ignis purgatione, quae fiat in adventu Christi secundo. Confer D. Joh. Crocium tractatu de purgatorio, aliosque nostrates.
english: XX. But Origen, laying the foundations of the papal purgatory from Plato's dogma, also expressed by Virgil in Aeneid book 6, first imported into the church a fire by which souls after this life would be purged from sins. XXI. Ambrose, Hilary, Jerome, and Rufinus followed Origen in this matter.

XXII. Yet Origen's purgatory differs from the papal in three ways. (1) By reason of persons: because according to the papalists only those are purged by fire whose souls are bound by the guilt of some temporal punishment, or who migrate from this life with some venial sins; but according to Origen and others who preceded Augustine, all mortals except Christ alone will undergo this fire. (2) By reason of time: because the papalists teach souls are to be purged by this fire immediately from departure, those ancients only on the last day of judgment. (3) By reason of mitigation: because the papalists judge that purgatorial punishments can be taken away or mitigated by the offerings and prayers of the living — which sort of thing Origen neither felt nor said, nor those we touch who followed him.

XXIII. Therefore purgatory such as the papalists hand down was unknown before Augustine's times: but to Augustine it seemed doubtful; yet from Gregory's age in the Roman church it has been held certain from lying revelations and visions; but the Greek church does not receive it even today. All these things Gerhard Vossius, a man of infinite reading and doctrine, has most rightly built up in On the State of the Separated Soul. If any things are brought from antiquity to the contrary, they are either from spurious and bastard writings, or they speak of the purgation of this age which is done by the fire of tribulation (as Augustine), or of the purgation of fire which may be done at Christ's second advent. Compare Doctor Johannes Crocius's treatise On Purgatory, and others of our people.

source_text: Suffragatur huic divisioni Irenaeus lib. 5. cap. 6. Chrysostomus hom. 13. ad Rom. Tertullianus initio libri de Trinitate & Athenagoras de resurrectione. Quae opinio si vera est, facilis est solutio omnium, quae contra animi immortalitatem ex scripturis afferuntur, & non multum absurdi continebit antiquorum psychopannychia bene intellecta, transeunte quasi in materiam animae anima non rationali sed sensitiva, ut corpora ex corporibus nascuntur. De qua materia inter antiquos ita Prudentius: Humus excipit arida corpus, animae rapit aura liquorem. Oraculum apud Pausaniam dicit, animam ferri in aethera. Ita Psellus, Graeci animam atermon ad elementa sublunaria, Chaldaei etiam supra lunam evehunt: Christiani vero etiam eam mori faciunt. Plutarchus, de facie in orbe Lun. pag. 174. Animarum, inquit, elementum luna est, solvuntur etenim in eam, quemadmodum in terram mortuorum corpora revertuntur. Sol vero recipit mentem, qui dedit eam. Antoninus denique lib. de vita sua pag. 36. hominem ex tribus constare, anima, corpore & spiritu a Stoicis traxerat: unde ait, mentem esse partem Dei ac proinde in coelum redire; de corpore autem & anima multis philosophatur, quibus recensendis hic supersedemus. Sensibilis igitur partis abolitio est altera cujusque animae a suo corpore discedentis plaga & mutatio, neque sane levis ista videbitur ei, qui hanc vulgi querimoniam apud Greg. Nyssenum considerat.
english: This division is supported by Irenaeus (book 5, chapter 6), Chrysostom (homily 13 on Romans), Tertullian at the beginning of On the Trinity, and Athenagoras On the Resurrection. If this opinion is true, the solution is easy of all things that are brought from the Scriptures against the immortality of the mind, and the ancients' soul-sleep, well understood, will contain not much absurdity — the sensitive soul, not the rational, passing as it were into the matter of the soul, as bodies are born from bodies. Concerning which matter Prudentius among the ancients thus: Dry soil receives the body; the breeze snatches the moisture of the soul. An oracle in Pausanias says the soul is carried into the ether. So Psellus: the Greeks carry the soul atermon to the sublunary elements; the Chaldeans even above the moon; but Christians even make it die. Plutarch, On the Face in the Moon's Orb (p. 174): The element of souls, he says, is the moon, for they are dissolved into it just as the bodies of the dead return into the earth. But the sun receives the mind, which gave it. Finally Antoninus in his book On His Life (p. 36) had drawn from the Stoics that the human being consists of three things — soul, body, and spirit: whence he says the mind is a part of God and therefore returns into heaven; but concerning body and soul he philosophizes much, which we here forbear to review. Therefore the abolition of the sensible part is the other plague and mutation of each soul departing from its body, nor indeed will this seem light to him who considers this complaint of the crowd in Gregory of Nyssa.

source_text: IX. Porro anima separata non exstinguitur, sed permanet. Irenaeus lib. 2. adversus haereses cap. 62. hoc potissimum educit e Christi narratione. Plenissime, inquiens, docuit Dominus perseverare animas in ea enarratione, quae scribitur de divite & de Lazaro, eo qui refrigerabatur in sinu Abrahae. Idem firmat Christus Matth. 22.32. Marc. 12.26.27. Matth. 10.28. & Luc. 12.4. & 23.43. & Stephanus Act. 7.59. & Paulus Rom. 8.11. & 14.8. Phil. 1.23. X. Anima separata non dormit, sed eorum meminit quae egit in hac vita, & quae sors se post judicium maneat novit, & vel felicitatis suae cogitatione gaudet, vel terribilis supplicii exspectatione torquetur. Hoc Irenaeus ibidem colligit. Plenissime, inquiens, Dominus docuit, non solum perseverare animas, sed & meminisse operum quae egerunt hic, & a quibus cessaverunt, in ea enarratione quae inscribitur de divite & Lazaro, in qua ait divitem cognoscere Lazarum post mortem, & Abrahamum similiter. Hoc idem firmant martyres Apoc. 6.10. & qui Agnum sequuntur, Apoc. 14.4. Unde & Cyprianus elegantissimo sermone de mortalitate: Magnus, inquit, illic nos charorum numerus exspectat, parentum, fratrum, filiorum frequens nos & copiosa turba desiderat, jam de sua immortalitate secura, & adhuc de nostra salute sollicita.
english: IX. Further, the separated soul is not extinguished, but remains. Irenaeus in Against Heresies book 2, chapter 62, draws this chiefly from Christ's narrative: Most fully, he says, the Lord taught that souls persevere in that narration which is written of the rich man and of Lazarus, who was refreshed in Abraham's bosom. The same Christ confirms (Matthew 22:32; Mark 12:26–27; Matthew 10:28; and Luke 12:4 and 23:43); and Stephen (Acts 7:59); and Paul (Romans 8:11 and 14:8; Philippians 1:23).

X. The separated soul does not sleep, but remembers the things it did in this life, and knows what lot awaits it after judgment, and either rejoices in the thought of its felicity or is tormented by the expectation of terrible punishment. Irenaeus gathers this in the same place: Most fully, he says, the Lord taught not only that souls persevere, but also that they remember the works which they did here and from which they ceased, in that narration which is inscribed of the rich man and Lazarus, in which he says the rich man recognizes Lazarus after death, and Abraham likewise. The same the martyrs confirm (Revelation 6:10) and those who follow the Lamb (Revelation 14:4). Whence also Cyprian in his most elegant sermon On Mortality: A great number of dear ones, he says, awaits us there; a frequent and abundant throng of parents, brothers, children desires us — already secure of their own immortality, and still anxious about our salvation.

source_text: VII. Tertia animae in morte plaga est, qua omnes operationes ejus, quae sunt praesertim ad extra, exstinguit. Nam imperfectum esse animae statum a corpore sejunctae, & nullum habere actum, multis sanctis viris visum est. Tatianus enim eo argumento probat animas non fieri daemones: quomodo forent animae operatrices post mortem? Anima ad agendum de suo minime sufficit, inquit Tertullianus lib. de resurr. cap. 46. Habet enim de suo solummodo cogitare, velle, cupere; ad perficiendum autem, operam carnis exspectat. Facta per carnem administrantur. Anima sola nihil facit, inquit Nyssenus orat. 1. de resurr. Spiritus hominis absque corpore nec ipse proficere, nec alteri prodesse potest, auctore Bernardo in Cant. serm. 5. Iterumque, ubi deerit corpus, delus non erit. Ita Durandus, quem Johannes Picus de Mirandula sequitur. Angeli dicuntur moveri de loco in locum, in quantum successive operantur in diversis locis. Anima autem separata non dicitur habere aliquam operationem circa locum, vel circa corpus existens in loco, quia cum ex natura sua sit determinata ad certum corpus, non potest movere, nec agere in aliud nisi mediante corpore proprio, sed illo caret, dum est separata. Ergo non potest anima moveri de loco ad locum ratione operationis.
english: VII. The third plague of the soul in death is that by which it extinguishes all its operations, especially those outward. For that the state of the soul severed from the body is imperfect, and that it has no act, has seemed so to many holy men. Tatian by that argument proves that souls do not become demons: how would souls be operative after death? The soul from its own resources scarcely suffices for acting, says Tertullian in On the Resurrection chapter 46. For from its own it has only to think, to will, to desire; but for accomplishing, it awaits the service of the flesh. Deeds are administered through the flesh. The soul alone does nothing, says Nyssen in the first oration On the Resurrection. The spirit of a human being without the body can neither itself advance nor profit another, as Bernard authorizes in Song of Songs sermon 5. And again, where the body shall be wanting, there will be no delusion. So Durandus, whom Pico della Mirandola follows. Angels are said to be moved from place to place insofar as they operate successively in diverse places. But the separated soul is not said to have any operation around a place, or around a body existing in a place, because since by its nature it is determined to a certain body, it cannot move nor act upon another except by means of its own body, but it lacks that while it is separated. Therefore the soul cannot be moved from place to place by reason of operation.

source_text: XII. Neque piorum gaudia, neque impiorum tormenta finiuntur: sed utrorumque status inde a morte, usque in diem judicii idem permanet, neque post exitum animae e corpore, homines quicquam emolumenti ulla hominum prudentia & studio percipere possunt. Hoc ex dictis Christi Luc. 16.26. colligunt Epiphanius haeres. 59. contra Catharos & Chrysostomus homil. 2. de Lazaro & auctor quaest. & respons. ad orthodoxos. Sic & Cyprianus tract. 1. ad Demetrianum f. 32. Quando isthinc excessum fuerit, nullus jam poenitentiae locus est, nullus satisfactionis effectus. Hacpropter quod Damascenus sive quicunque alius scriptor orationis de iis, qui cum fide ex hac vita excesserunt, animam Falconillae, quanquam sine lavacro & fide mortuae, precibus tamen Theclae dicit fuisse servatam: id sacrarum literarum & purioris antiquitatis judicio repugnat. XIII. Neque animae, inde quo semel fuerit delata, regressus in terras ulla virtute magica conceditur. Hoc concludit Tertullianus e verbis Christi jam laudatis, lib. de anima cap. 57. Satis, inquiens, Dominus in argumento illo pauperis quiescentis & divitis ingemiscentis ex persona Abrahae sanxit, non posse relegari renunciatorem dispositionis infernae: quod vel tunc licere potuisset, ut Mosi & prophetis crederetur. Sed etsi quasdam revocavit in corpora Dei virtus, in documenta juris sui, non idcirco communicabitur fidei & audaciae magarum, & fallaciae somniorum, & licentiae poetarum.
english: XII. Neither the joys of the pious nor the torments of the impious are finished: but the status of both remains the same from death until the day of judgment, nor after the soul's exit from the body can humans perceive any benefit by any prudence and study of humans. This from Christ's words in Luke 16:26 Epiphanius gathers (Heresy 59 against the Cathars) and Chrysostom (homily 2 on Lazarus) and the author of Questions and Responses to the Orthodox. So also Cyprian in tract 1 to Demetrianus (folio 32): When departure from here shall have occurred, there is already no place of penitence, no effect of satisfaction. For that reason what Damascene — or whoever else is the writer of the oration concerning those who have departed this life with faith — says, that the soul of Falconilla, although dead without washing and faith, was yet saved by Thecla's prayers: that conflicts with the judgment of the sacred letters and of purer antiquity.

XIII. Nor is return to the lands granted to a soul, from where it has once been carried, by any magical power. Tertullian concludes this from Christ's words already praised, in On the Soul chapter 57: Enough, he says, has the Lord sanctioned in that argument of the resting poor man and the groaning rich man from Abraham's person, that a messenger of the infernal disposition cannot be relegated: which might even then have been permitted, that Moses and the prophets might be believed. But although God's power recalled some into bodies for proofs of his right, it will not therefore be communicated to the faith and boldness of sorceresses, and the deceit of dreams, and the license of poets.

source_text: VIII. Ultima animae in morte plaga est, quae illi aestuans quoddam, anodon absque dolore tamen, desiderium infigit, felicitatis una cum resumto corpore consummandae. Hinc Bernhardus de concept. s. de diligendo Deo: Animae solutae, inquit, etiam sanctorum ligatae corporibus sunt, etsi non vita vel sensu, certe affectu naturali, ita ut absque his nec velint nec valeant consummari. Et serm. 4. in fest. sanct. Non erit integra beatitudo, donec integer homo cuidetur. Neque sane leviter de hac privatione censendum est. Magnam quandam in ea poenam Tertullianus agnoscere videtur lib. de anima in fine. In summa, inquiens, cum carcerem illum quem Euangelium demonstrat, inferos intelligimus, & novissimum quadrantem modicum quoque dilatum mora resurrectionis illic luendum interpretamur: nemo dubitabit animam aliquid pensare penes inferos, salva resurrectionis plenitudine per carnem quoque. Atque sane, vehemens earum ad corpora desiderium est. Ideo in Apocalypsi sub altari etiam clamantes introducuntur, de quo Gregorius expos. moral. in cap. 1. Jobi lib. 2. cap. 4. Quid est animas vindictae petitionem dicere, nisi diem extremum judicii & resurrectionem extinctorum corporum desiderare? Magnus quippe earum clamor, magnum est desiderium. Et Bernhardus serm. 3. domin. de ramis palmarum: A labore quiescunt, qui in Domino moriuntur, sed non quiescunt interim a clamore. Denique sub throno Dei clamant animae occisorum, quia, etsi nihil habent quod molestet, nondum tamen habent quod delectet, donec requiem resurrectio, donec sabbatum pascha sequatur.
english: VIII. The last plague of the soul in death is that which implants in her a certain burning — painless yet — desire of felicity to be consummated together with the resumed body. Hence Bernard in the treatise On Loving God: The freed souls, he says, even of the saints are bound to bodies — if not by life or sense, certainly by natural affection — so that without these they neither will nor are able to be consummated. And in sermon 4 on the feast of the saints: There will not be integral beatitude until the whole human being is cared for. Nor indeed is this privation to be lightly estimated. Tertullian seems to acknowledge a certain great punishment in it at the end of On the Soul: In sum, he says, when we understand by that prison which the Gospel demonstrates the inferi, and interpret the last farthing — a little also deferred by the delay of the resurrection — as to be paid there: no one will doubt that the soul pays something among the inferi, the fullness of the resurrection through the flesh also being safe.

And indeed their desire toward bodies is vehement. Therefore in the Apocalypse they are even introduced crying under the altar, concerning which Gregory in the Moral Exposition on Job chapter 1, book 2, chapter 4: What is it to say that souls petition for vengeance, except to desire the last day of judgment and the resurrection of extinguished bodies? For their great cry is a great desire. And Bernard in sermon 3 on Palm Sunday: Those who die in the Lord rest from labor, but they do not meanwhile rest from crying. Finally under the throne of God the souls of the slain cry, because although they have nothing that molests, they do not yet have what delights, until the resurrection follows rest, until Passover follows the sabbath.

source_text: VI. Secunda animae in morte plaga est, quae partem illam, quae est nobis cum brutis communis, illi eripit. Quam privationem ut intelligamus, nonnulla nobis ex aliorum opinionibus hic repetenda videntur. Paulus Heb. 4.12. habet divisionem animae & spiritus, ex quo licet conjicere, non omnino inepte philosophatos veteres, qui tria in homine constituebant, mentem, animam & corpus, quorum duo posteriora mortalia etiam affirmabant. Neque enim animae humanae immortalitati quicquam derogare visum Gregorio Nysseno de anima & resurrectione, cum ta thymika kai epithymetika interire dicerentur: utpote quae non ex animae essentia esse, sed extrinsecus advenientia, & quasi posita in animae confinio, his ostendat rationibus: 1. Quicquid a Deo alienum, id etiam ab animae definitione, quae nihil admittit nisi proprium. 2. Ratio contra haec pugnat, ab his se segregat quantum licet. Natura autem civile bellum non exercet. 3. Habent ista causas ex corpore, ut iracundia fervore sanguinis. Confer Ambrosium de paradiso cap. 1. & 2. Eandem divisionem Origenes in Matth. 24.51. ita ponit: Dividit eum, inquiens, quando spiritus quidem ejus revertitur ad Deum, qui dedit eum, anima autem cum corpore suo vadit in gehennam. Justus autem non dividitur, sed anima ejus vadit cum spiritu ad regna coelestia. Huc spectat quod Hieronymus in cap. 5. Ephes. scribit, se spiritus mortem nequaquam legere, animae frequenter.
english: VI. The second plague of the soul in death is that which snatches from her that part which is common to us with the brutes. That we may understand this privation, some things from others' opinions seem here to be repeated. Paul in Hebrews 4:12 has a division of soul and spirit, from which one may conjecture that the ancients did not altogether foolishly philosophize who constituted three things in the human being — mind, soul, and body — of which they also affirmed the two latter to be mortal.

Nor did Gregory of Nyssa in On the Soul and Resurrection seem to derogate anything from the immortality of the human soul when the irascible and concupiscible parts were said to perish: inasmuch as they are not of the essence of the soul but adventitious from without and as it were placed on the soul's boundary, he shows by these reasons: (1) Whatever is alien from God is also alien from the definition of the soul, which admits nothing except what is proper. (2) Reason fights against these and segregates itself from them as far as it may; but nature does not wage civil war. (3) These have causes from the body, as anger from the heat of blood. Compare Ambrose, On Paradise, chapters 1 and 2. Origen places the same division on Matthew 24:51: He divides him, he says, when his spirit indeed returns to God who gave it, but the soul goes with its body into gehenna. But the just man is not divided, but his soul goes with the spirit to the heavenly kingdoms. To this looks what Jerome writes on Ephesians chapter 5, that he nowhere reads of the death of the spirit, frequently of the soul.

source_text: V. Prima plaga est, quae corpus ab ipsa avellit, quocum charissimo foederis vinculo jam inde ab ortu consociata fuit. Quod infelix divortium non solum flebiliter lamentari impii solent, ut Adrianus imperator Romanus: Animula vagula, blandula, hospes comesque corporis, quae nunc abis in loca? Pallidula, frigida, nudula, nec ut soles dabis jocos. Sed pii etiam, quanquam ad Dominum se migraturos certo sciunt, aegre ferunt, sicuti contestatur Paulus, 2.Cor. 5.2. Nollemus exui, sed magis ut mortalitas a vita absorberetur, sine ulla morte scilicet, sicut iis demum continget, qui Domini adventu ultimo in vivis fuerint. De hoc, deque his inferis Tertullianus lib. de carne Christi cap. 42. Quis, inquit, non desiderabit, dum in carne est, superinduere immortalitatem & continuare vitam, lucrifacta morte, per vicariam demutationem, ne inferos experiatur usque novissimum quadrantem exoluturos? Ceterum demutationem etiam post resurrectionem consecuturus est, inferos jam expertus.
english: V. The first plague is that which tears the body away from her, with which she had been associated from birth by the dearest bond of covenant. This unhappy divorce the impious are accustomed not only to lament tearfully — as Hadrian the Roman emperor: Little soul, wandering, charming, guest and companion of the body, where now do you go? Pale, cold, naked, nor will you give jokes as you used to — but the pious also, although they certainly know they will migrate to the Lord, bear it ill, as Paul testifies (2 Corinthians 5:2): We would not be unclothed, but rather that mortality might be swallowed up by life, without any death namely, as will finally befall those who at the Lord's last coming shall be among the living.

Concerning this, and concerning these inferi, Tertullian in On the Flesh of Christ chapter 42: Who, he says, will not desire, while he is in the flesh, to put on immortality over it and to continue life, having gained by death through a vicarious change, lest he experience the inferi that will exact even to the last farthing? For the rest, he will attain the change also after the resurrection, having already experienced the inferi.

source_text: XIV. Positiva receptaque veterum ad nostrum usque Sardeniense saeculum sententia fuit, animas fidelium veteris testamenti non prius in paradisum fuisse receptas, quam cum morte sua reserasset Christus, primusque illum cum latrone esset ingressus. Haec vero est inter eas quaestiones, ob quas minime turbari aut scindi debeat Ecclesia, auctore Calvino l. 4. inst. cap. 1. §. 12. praesertim si in eo consensus sit, quod animae patrum veterum statim ab excessu beatitudine ac benefica Dei praesentia potirentur. Theophilus Antiochenus inter antiquos lib. 4. Alleg. In his quoque, ait, quod apud infernum Abrahamum videt, haec subesse a quibusdam ratio putatur, quod omnes sancti ante adventum Domini Jesu Christi etiam ad inferna, licet in refrigerii locum, descendisse dicuntur. Sic Jo. Chrysostomus hom. 4. in Marcum, Hieronymus ad Heliodorum in epitaphio Nepotiani, item ad Paulam super obitu Blesillae & ad Ecclesiasten cap. 3. & 9. Augustinus lib. 20. de C.D. cap. 15. & ep. 99. ad Evodium, Concilium Toletanum sub Honorio anno 633. celebratum, cap. 1. Descendit, inquit, ad inferos, ut sanctos, qui ibidem tenebantur, erueret: quam sententiam clare item asserunt Irenaeus, Tertullianus, Origenes, Gregorius Neocaesariensis, Eusebius, Macarius Hierosolymitanus, Basilius, Athanasius, Epiphanius, Cyrillus Hieros., Ambrosius, Rufinus, Synesius, imo & e junioribus Zwinglius in epist. ad Heb. 11.39.40. Calvinus in psychopannychia, Bullingerus ad Luc. 16.23. & Heb. 9.8. & 1.Pet. 3.19. & Martyr ad 2.Reg. 2.13.
english: XIV. The positive and received sentence of the ancients down to our Sardian age was that the souls of the faithful of the Old Testament were not received into paradise before Christ by his death had unlocked it and first entered it with the thief. But this is among those questions on account of which the Church ought least to be troubled or split, as Calvin authorizes (Institutes book 4, chapter 1, §12) — especially if there is consensus in this, that the souls of the ancient fathers immediately from their departure obtained beatitude and the beneficent presence of God. Theophilus of Antioch among the ancients (Allegories book 4): In these things also, he says, that he sees Abraham among the infernal, this reason is thought by some to underlie, that all the saints before the advent of the Lord Jesus Christ are said to have descended even to the inferi, though into a place of refreshment.

So John Chrysostom (homily 4 on Mark), Jerome to Heliodorus in the epitaph of Nepotianus, likewise to Paula on the death of Blesilla and on Ecclesiastes chapters 3 and 9, Augustine (City of God book 20, chapter 15, and letter 99 to Evodius), the Council of Toledo under Honorius celebrated in the year 633 (chapter 1): He descended, it says, to the inferi, that he might rescue the saints who were held there — which sentence clearly also assert Irenaeus, Tertullian, Origen, Gregory of Neocaesarea, Eusebius, Macarius of Jerusalem, Basil, Athanasius, Epiphanius, Cyril of Jerusalem, Ambrose, Rufinus, Synesius, and even among the juniors Zwingli on Hebrews 11:39–40, Calvin in the Psychopannychia, Bullinger on Luke 16:23 and Hebrews 9:8 and 1 Peter 3:19, and Martyr on 2 Kings 2:13.

source_text: XV. Patres, qui vixere ante annum Christi quadringentesimum, judicarunt animas fidelium, postquam Christus paradisum aperuisset, statim ab excessu recipi in paradisum. XVI. Sed in loquendi ratione multum differre videntur, quia alii eas dicunt confestim in coelum recipi, alii volunt ad extremum usque diem apud inferos detineri. XVII. Quanquam autem nihil magis diversum a coelo videatur, quam inferi: tamen, si patrum istorum mentem potius, quam verba ponderemus, non inter haec tantam comperiemus antilegian contradictionem, quam videtur. Nam sub inferorum nomine non intelligunt tormentorum locum, sed vel communiorem (sic vocant) animarum separatarum statum, vel locum invisibilem a Deo definitum, quem alii statuunt infra, alii intra terram, alii extra mundum, alii etiam ignotum hominibus putant. Vide Sanfordum & Parkerum lib. 2. de descensu ad inferos sect. 44. 45. 53. 54. 55. XVIII. In eo vero conveniunt omnes, quod animae in hocce statu, de gloriae consummatione certe, beatam resurrectionem cum gaudio exspectent. XIX. Neque recte facturi videmur, si patribus illis, vel aliis, qui hactenus consentiunt, eo nomine tanquam male catholicis, controversiam moveamus. Vide doctissimum Gerh. Vossium de statu animae separatae q. 2. th. 5. Hugonem Sanfordum & Robertum Parkerum quatuor eruditissimis libris de descensu D. N. Jesu Christi ad inferos hanc magnam quaestionem de inferno ex antiquis solide edisserentes.
english: XV. The fathers who lived before the four-hundredth year of Christ judged that the souls of the faithful, after Christ had opened paradise, are received into paradise immediately from their departure.
XVI. But in the manner of speaking they seem to differ much, because some say they are received at once into heaven, others will have them detained among the inferi even to the last day.

XVII. Although nothing seems more diverse from heaven than the inferi: yet if we weigh those fathers' mind rather than their words, we shall not find among these so great a contradiction as it seems. For under the name of the inferi they do not understand a place of torments, but either the more common (so they call it) status of separated souls, or an invisible place defined by God, which some place below, some within the earth, some outside the world, some even think unknown to humans. See Sanford and Parker, On the Descent to Hell, book 2, sections 44, 45, 53, 54, 55.
XVIII. But in this all agree, that souls in this status certainly await with joy the blessed resurrection concerning the consummation of glory.

XIX. Nor do we seem about to do rightly if on that account we move controversy against those fathers, or others who thus far agree, as if they were badly catholic. See the most learned Gerhard Vossius On the State of the Separated Soul, question 2, thesis 5; Hugh Sanford and Robert Parker in four most erudite books On the Descent of Our Lord Jesus Christ to Hell, solidly discussing this great question of hell from the ancients.

source_text: IV. Hujus communis status quatuor sunt gradus: 1. Animae a corpore suo divortium. 2. partis sensitivae amissio. 3. actionum ad extra privatio. 4. defectus gloriae consummatae per resumtionem corporis, quae totidem illius mutationes, plagae & quasi vulnera dici possunt.
english: IV. Of this common status there are four grades: (1) the soul's divorce from its body; (2) the loss of the sensitive part; (3) the privation of outward actions; (4) the defect of consummated glory pending the resumption of the body — which may be called so many of its mutations, plagues, and as it were wounds.

source_text: Solutarum vero animarum statum non tam exprimit nobis, quam adumbrat vox aedes figuratae accepta. Nam de futurae vitae statu, quod ad animam spectat, nihil fere in sacris proprie enunciatur. Recte enim Irenaeus l. 2. cap. 35. terrena, ait, congruit typos esse eorum, quae sunt coelestia, ab eodem tamen Deo facta. Neque enim aliter potuerunt assimilari spirituales imagines. Quid hoc? Non aliter possunt nisi figurate edoceri coelestia. Cujus rei rationem reddere Gregorius Nyssenus videtur. Neque vero, inquiens, quis mihi figuram habitumque & formam describat, illius non manu facti domicilii, ad similitudinem earum figurarum quae nunc apparent in nobis. Cum enim non solum resurrectio nobis a sacris literis praedicata sit, verum etiam immutatio promissa: omnino necesse est absconditum esse & prorsus ignorari in quid immutabimur: quippe cum nullum exemplum, nullaque similitudo eorum, quae sperantur in vita, conspiciatur. Vide Sanfordum lib. 2. de descensu ad inferos f. 43. & 44. II. Status animae separatae duplex est, communis aut proprius. III. Communis est, animae cujusque ex hoc visibili mundo per solutionem a corpore suo discessio.
english: But the state of freed souls Scripture does not so much express to us as adumbrate by the word house taken figuratively. For concerning the state of the future life, as it regards the soul, almost nothing is properly enunciated in the sacred writings. Rightly indeed Irenaeus (book 2, chapter 35) says it is fitting that earthly things be types of those that are heavenly, yet made by the same God. For spiritual images could not otherwise be assimilated. What is this? Heavenly things cannot otherwise be taught except figuratively. Gregory of Nyssa seems to give the reason of this matter: Nor indeed, he says, let anyone describe to me the figure, habit, and form of that dwelling not made by hand, after the likeness of those figures which now appear in us. For since not only is the resurrection preached to us from the sacred letters, but also a change is promised: it is altogether necessary that it be hidden and utterly unknown into what we shall be changed — inasmuch as no example and no likeness of the things hoped for is seen in this life. See Sanford, On the Descent to Hell, book 2, folios 43 and 44.
II. The state of the separated soul is twofold, common or proper.
III. The common state is each soul's departure from this visible world by dissolution from its body.

source_text: XI. Haec de statu communi: proprius animarum, cum de saeculo exierunt, itidem duplex est, status gaudii seu regni coelorum, quo excipiuntur animae piorum, & tormenti, in quem traduntur animae impiorum, qui eodem sensu gehenna dicitur, lib. 5. hypognosticorum. Sic docet Christus Matth. 25.34.41. Marc. 16.16. Luc. 16.23. Joh. 3.18. Hinc Irenaeus lib. 5. cap. 27. duos mortuorum ordines faciens, dicit impios & blasphemos in aeternum ignem mitti, justis & aequis vitam donari & claritatem aeternam circumdari. Tertullianus quoque idem colligit lib. de idololatria cap. 13. Si cum saeculo gaudemus, verendum est ne cum saeculo hinc lugeamus. Saeculo autem gaudente lugeamus, & saeculo postea lugente gaudebimus. Sic Lazarus in sinu Abrahae refrigerium consecuturus, contra dives in tormento ignis consolatus alternas malorum & bonorum vices aemula retributione compensat. Neque praeter hosce duos tertius defunctorum locus & status est, nec aliter Fulgentius ad Venantium de poenitentia cap. 7. Ut, inquit, noverimus illos qui gaudiis temporalibus oblectantur & jussa divina contemnunt, aeternis ignibus cremandos: illos vero qui mala temporalia cum timore Dei patienter tolerant aeterna quiete potituros: attendamus divitem purpuratum & pauperem Lazarum. Neque est quod dicatur, haec post resurrectionem quidem habere locum, ante eam non item. Nam, ut vere Olympiodorus in Eccles. 1.3. In quocunque, ait, loco deprehendatur homo cum moritur, in eo gradu atque ordine permanet in aeternum. Et Augustinus epist. 80. ad Hesychium: In quo quemque invenerit suus novissimus dies, in hoc eum comprehendet mundi novissimus dies. Et serm. de tempore 232. Nemo se decipiat, fratres. Duo enim loca sunt, & tertius non est ullus. Qui cum Christo regnare non meruerit, cum diabolo absque dubitatione ulla peribit.
english: XI. These things concerning the common status: the proper status of souls, when they have gone out from the age, is likewise twofold — the status of joy or of the kingdom of the heavens, by which the souls of the pious are received, and of torment, into which the souls of the impious are delivered, which in the same sense is called gehenna (Hypognostics book 5). So Christ teaches (Matthew 25:34, 41; Mark 16:16; Luke 16:23; John 3:18). Hence Irenaeus (book 5, chapter 27), making two orders of the dead, says the impious and blasphemers are sent into eternal fire, while to the just and equitable life is given and eternal brightness is put around them. Tertullian also gathers the same in On Idolatry chapter 13: If we rejoice with the age, it is to be feared lest we mourn with the age hereafter. But let us mourn while the age rejoices, and we shall rejoice when the age afterward mourns.

So Lazarus is about to obtain refreshment in Abraham's bosom; on the contrary the rich man, comforted in the torment of fire, compensates alternating turns of evils and goods by rival retribution. Nor besides these two is there a third place and status of the dead, nor otherwise Fulgentius to Venantius On Penitence chapter 7: That we may know, he says, that those who delight in temporal joys and contemn divine commands are to be burned with eternal fires, but those who patiently bear temporal evils with the fear of God will obtain eternal rest: let us attend to the purple-clad rich man and poor Lazarus. Nor is it to be said that these things have place after the resurrection indeed, but not before it. For as Olympiodorus truly says on Ecclesiastes 1:3: In whatever place a human being is found when he dies, in that grade and order he remains forever. And Augustine to Hesychius (letter 80): In what state each one's own last day finds him, in that the last day of the world will seize him. And sermon On Time 232: Let no one deceive himself, brothers. For there are two places, and there is no third. Whoever has not deserved to reign with Christ will perish with the devil without any doubt.

source_text: Sic Hermes in Asclep. p. 61. Mors, ait, mutatio est, eo quod corpus quidem solvitur, vita vero in obscurum abit, sic pars mundi aliqua quotidie fit invisibilis. Corporis mors est, cum ab anima, animae, cum a Deo derelinquitur. Quemadmodum autem abeunte anima, corpus non illud quidem in nihilum redit, sed omnem humanitatis naturam deperdit: sic & anima discedente Deo, ne illa esse quidem definit, sed definit esse quod fuit, nec jam anima est, si verum liceat dicere, sed ut ita dicam, cadaver animae. Nec miretur quispiam, quod corruptionem etiam animae tributam audiat supra cap. 1. scholio aph. 7. Praeter enim omnis boni privationem, quae maxima est corruptio, quam damnatorum animae patiuntur: & in beatissimis, donec resumtis corporibus consummantur, privatio est, defectus est, ac proinde corruptio est, quanquam longe distans ab ea, quam impiorum animae experiuntur. Neque enim in ipsis corporibus eadem est corruptionis ratio. Solvuntur piorum corpora, sed ut coelestem induant naturam: impiorum, ut quod habuerunt boni amittant: idcirco in terram hanc nostram primum diffluunt, ex illa rursum in spiritualem terram aeternae corruptionis transitura. Animarum eadem ratio: regnat in omnibus ad tempus privationis vis, sed piorum animae deficiendo proficiunt, impiorum naturalis casus aeterno praecipitio terminatur.
english: So Hermes in the Asclepius (p. 61): Death, he says, is a change, because the body indeed is dissolved, but life goes away into obscurity, so that some part of the world daily becomes invisible. The death of the body is when it is forsaken by the soul; of the soul, when it is forsaken by God. And just as when the soul departs the body does not indeed return into nothing, but loses the whole nature of humanity: so also when God departs the soul does not indeed cease to be, but ceases to be what it was, and is no longer a soul, if one may say truly, but — so to speak — a corpse of a soul.

Nor let anyone wonder that corruption is attributed also to the soul above in chapter 1, scholium on aphorism 7. For besides the privation of every good, which is the greatest corruption, which the souls of the damned suffer: even in the most blessed, until they are consummated with bodies resumed, there is privation, there is defect, and therefore there is corruption — though far distant from that which the souls of the impious experience. Nor indeed in the bodies themselves is the reason of corruption the same. The bodies of the pious are dissolved, but that they may put on a heavenly nature; of the impious, that they may lose what good they had: therefore they first melt away into this our earth, from that again to pass into a spiritual earth of eternal corruption. The same reason holds of souls: the force of privation reigns in all for a time, but the souls of the pious by failing advance, while the natural fall of the impious is terminated in eternal precipice.
